title: "Elastic Constants: E, ν, λ, μ"

## Conversion table for isotropic elastic constants

In the lecture notes, (1.13) and (1.14) give the relationship between the pair $(E,\nu)$ and $(\mu, \lambda)$. You can find a full relationship table between each parameters on Wikipedia.

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Template:Elastic_moduli

We reproduce it with only $E,\nu,\mu,\lambda$ to make it more readable.

| Given | $E$ | $\nu$ | $\lambda$ | $\mu$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| $(E,\nu)$ | – | – | $\dfrac{E\nu}{(1+\nu)(1-2\nu)}$ | $\dfrac{E}{2(1+\nu)}$ |
| $(E,\lambda)$ | – | $\dfrac{2\lambda}{E+\lambda+R}$| – | $\dfrac{E-3\lambda+R}{4}$ |
| $(E,\mu)$ | – | $\dfrac{E}{2\mu}-1$ | $\dfrac{\mu(E-2\mu)}{3\mu-E}$ | – |
| $(\nu,\lambda)$ | $\dfrac{\lambda(1+\nu)(1-2\nu)}{\nu}$ | – | – | $\dfrac{\lambda(1-2\nu)}{2\nu}$ |
| $(\nu,\mu)$ | $2\mu(1+\nu)$ | – | $\dfrac{2\mu\nu}{1-2\nu}$ | – |
| $(\lambda,\mu)$ | $\dfrac{\mu(3\lambda+2\mu)}{\lambda+\mu}$ | $\dfrac{\lambda}{2(\lambda+\mu)}$ | – | – |

: $R=\pm \sqrt{E^2+9\lambda^2+2E\lambda}$.

## Poisson's ratio — what does it mean?

Pull a bar and it usually gets thinner — that lateral response is set by $\nu$. Try the
presets below: cork ($\nu\approx0$), typical metals ($\nu\approx0.3$), rubber
($\nu\approx0.499$, nearly incompressible), and auxetic foam ($\nu<0$, gets *fatter*
when stretched).

{{< include ../interactives/_poisson_intuition.md >}}

## Lamé constants ↔ (E, ν)

$$
\mu = \frac{E}{2(1+\nu)}, \qquad \lambda = \frac{E\nu}{(1+\nu)(1-2\nu)}, \qquad K = \frac{E}{3(1-2\nu)}
$$

{{< include ../interactives/_lame_constants.md >}}

## What do λ and μ mean physically?

$\mu$ resists pure shape change (shear). $\lambda$ is subtler — it's the stress that
appears sideways *only when lateral strain is prevented* (confined loading), not something
you'd feel in a free pull test.

{{< include ../interactives/_lame_intuition.md >}}
